notes.b: Nagy was a Hungarian communist who became the hope of reformers inside the party. He led the government during the uprising and paid for it with his life. He is a 30-mark Ordinary Level question and features in Higher answers.
points: Born in 1896, Nagy was a communist who lived in the Soviet Union from 1930 to 1944 and returned in 1944 with the Red Army. He was minister of agriculture in 1944-45, carrying out the 1945 land reform that gave estates to peasants, then interior minister in 1945-46.

He was prime minister from July 1953 to April 1955, appointed after Soviet leaders criticised Rákosi at a meeting in Moscow in June 1953. His New Course meant more consumer goods, less forced industrialisation, peasants allowed to leave collective farms, internment camps closed and some prisoners freed.

Rákosi stayed party first secretary and worked against Nagy, which divided the communists. Malenkov's fall in Moscow in February 1955 weakened Nagy, and Rákosi had him removed in April 1955 and expelled late that year after he criticised collectivisation and heavy industry.

Out of office he became the focus of reform-minded communists and intellectuals, which is why students demanded him on 22 October. Readmitted to the party in October 1956, he was reappointed prime minister on 24 October but was slow at first to side with the insurgents.

He then accepted their demands (ceasefire, an end to the AVH, multi-party government), declared neutrality on 1 November and appealed to the United Nations. On 4 November he broadcast that Soviet troops were attacking Budapest and took refuge in the Yugoslav embassy.

He left the embassy on 22 November under a written guarantee of safe conduct from Kádár's government, was seized by Soviet forces and taken to Romania, tried in secret and executed on 16 June 1958 with Pál Maléter and the journalist Miklós Gimes. He was buried in an unmarked grave.
Contemporaries disagreed: Moscow and Kádár called him a traitor and counter-revolutionary, the insurgents and the West saw a national hero, and some insurgents distrusted him as a communist.

Historians now see a reform communist carried along by events rather than their organiser, and debate his naivety about Soviet intentions. He was rehabilitated and reburied in Budapest on 16 June 1989, the thirty-first anniversary of his execution, before a huge crowd.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for Nagy's career in order with dates (24 October, 30 October, 1 November, 4 November) and his fate: embassy, abduction, secret trial, execution in 1958. Higher Level answers must also judge him, so weigh reformer carried by events against leader, and naive against principled.

notes.h: Background: a satellite state under Soviet control
notes.b: To understand why Hungary rose up, start with what Hungary had become after the war: a country formally independent but run in Moscow's interest.
points: Hungary fought as Germany's ally in the Second World War. The Red Army took Budapest in February 1945 after a long siege and Soviet troops stayed in Hungary after the war, which meant Moscow had force on the spot.

Communist control was complete by 1948-49, reached by what Rákosi is usually said to have called salami tactics (cutting opponents away slice by slice). It ended in the one-party Hungarian People's Republic of 1949.
A satellite state is a country that is formally independent but controlled by the Soviet Union in politics, economy and defence. Hungary was the textbook example.

Sovietisation means remaking a country on the Soviet model: one-party rule, a secret police, planned heavy industry, collectivised farms (peasants forced to pool land into state-run units), Soviet-style culture and loyalty to Moscow.

The Warsaw Pact, signed on 14 May 1955, bound Hungary militarily to the Soviet Union as a founding member. In the same month the Austrian State Treaty made Austria neutral and Soviet troops left it, which made neutrality look possible to Hungarians.

Stalin died in March 1953 and an uncertain collective leadership took over in Moscow. This opened the way for de-Stalinisation, the retreat from Stalin's terror and cult of personality, which began after 1953 and gathered pace after 1956.
notes.tip: Define satellite state and Sovietisation in one sentence each and apply them to Hungary, because the Higher Level question on how far Sovietisation succeeded rewards using Hungary as evidence.

notes.h: Causes: Rákosi's Stalinist rule and national resentment
notes.b: The long-term causes were the way Rákosi governed, the hardship it caused and the sense that Hungary was ruled from abroad. Each fed resentment that needed only a trigger.
points: Mátyás Rákosi led the Hungarian communists and ran a one-party state with a personality cult, show trials (staged trials with a fixed verdict) and purges. László Rajk, a former interior minister, was executed in October 1949 after one.

The AVH, the State Protection Authority (Államvédelmi Hatóság, earlier called the ÁVO), was the secret police. It spied on and arrested ordinary citizens and was the best-known instrument of Rákosi's rule and the main target of popular hatred.

The regime also attacked the churches. Cardinal József Mindszenty, head of the Catholic Church in Hungary, was arrested in December 1948, put on show trial in February 1949 and sentenced to life imprisonment.

The economy was run on Soviet lines. Forced collectivisation and heavy industry under the first five-year plan (from 1950) were favoured over consumer goods, so living standards fell, which fuelled resentment among workers and peasants.
Hungary also paid war reparations to the Soviet Union and had economic obligations to supply it, which kept living standards low. These burdens meant ordinary Hungarians paid for Soviet recovery.

National feeling added to the anger. Soviet troops remained, Soviet-style culture was imposed and Russian was a compulsory school subject. Hungarians remembered the 1848 revolution, and the poet Sándor Petőfi, its hero, was a national symbol.
notes.tip: On causes questions, marks go for a chain from long-term cause to trigger, not a list. Name people and dates for each cause, for example Rajk's execution in 1949 and Mindszenty's trial in 1949.

notes.h: Causes: the split in the party and the ferment of 1956
notes.b: From 1953 the communist leadership itself was divided, and in 1956 a series of shocks showed Hungarians that change was possible. These were the medium-term causes and the triggers.
points: Nagy's New Course of 1953 against Rákosi's hard line showed that change was possible, and it divided the communists. Nagy's fall in April 1955 turned him into a focus for reformers.
Khrushchev's secret speech to the Twentieth Party Congress on 25 February 1956 exposed the crimes of Stalin's era. It gave Hungarian reformers a precedent for criticising their own leaders.
The Petőfi Circle, a discussion club of reform-minded young communists and intellectuals set up in 1955, held large public debates in summer 1956. The Writers' Union also demanded change.
Rákosi was forced to resign as party leader on 18 July 1956, with the Soviet leader Anastas Mikoyan present in Budapest. He was replaced by Ernő Gerő, another Stalinist, who lacked popular support.

Rajk was reburied on 6 October 1956 before a very large crowd, which turned the memory of the regime's crimes into a public demonstration. This is why it counts as a trigger: it showed the regime's victims openly.

The Polish October encouraged Hungarians. Władysław Gomułka was elected Polish party leader on 21 October 1956 after Khrushchev visited Warsaw, and Soviet troops were not used, so Hungarians hoped for the same.
notes.tip: Sort the causes into long-term (Rákosi, the AVH, hardship), medium-term (the New Course and Nagy's fall) and triggers (the secret speech, Rákosi's removal, the Rajk reburial, the Polish October and the 22-23 October events). Examiners reward that structure.

notes.b: A student protest in Budapest turned into a national uprising within a day, because the regime answered the crowd with gunfire.
points: On 22 October students at the Technical University in Budapest drew up sixteen points. They demanded the withdrawal of Soviet troops, Imre Nagy as prime minister, free elections with several parties, freedom of speech and press, and the removal of the Stalin statue.
On 23 October a march went to the statue of General József Bem (a Polish-born hero of 1848) in sympathy with Poland, and then to Parliament, where a huge crowd gathered.

Gerő's radio speech that evening condemned the demonstrators, which angered the crowd rather than calming it. Part of the crowd pulled down the Stalin statue in Budapest, and its boots were left on the plinth.
A delegation tried to broadcast the demands from the Radio Budapest building, and the AVH fired on the crowd outside it. Fighting began across Budapest.

Armed civilians and army units joined the fighting. Soviet troops already in Hungary entered Budapest in the early hours of 24 October, and the Gerő government had asked Moscow for help. The uprising spread to other towns in the following days.
notes.tip: Keep the dates and places apart: 22 October is the students' demands, 23 October the demonstration, and the Bem statue, Stalin statue and radio building are three different places. The march began at the Bem statue, and the first shots were at the radio building.

notes.b: In four days a government crisis became an armed revolution, with Nagy trying to steer it while the Soviet tanks were still in the streets.
points: Nagy was reappointed prime minister on 24 October, and Kádár replaced Gerő as party first secretary on 25 October. Soviet leaders Mikoyan and Mikhail Suslov were in Budapest during the crisis, and Yuri Andropov was Soviet ambassador.
On 25 October security forces and Soviet tanks fired on the crowd in Kossuth Square outside Parliament, and many were killed. The shooting hardened feeling against the regime.
Insurgents held strongholds such as the Corvin Passage. Colonel Pál Maléter, sent to the Kilián barracks, went over to the insurgents.

Revolutionary committees (local bodies that took over administration) and workers' councils (elected by factory workers to run their workplaces) formed across the country. Some councils organised strikes and demanded genuine workers' control.

A ceasefire followed, and in his broadcast of 28 October Nagy called the rising a national democratic movement, not a counter-revolution. He promised that the AVH would be dissolved and Soviet troops would leave Budapest.
notes.tip: Quote Nagy's 28 October broadcast by content, not in quotation marks: a national democratic movement, the AVH to be dissolved, Soviet troops to leave Budapest. Do not mix up Kossuth Square (25 October shooting) with Republic Square (30 October lynchings).

notes.h: Soviet withdrawal and multi-party government: 29-31 October
notes.b: For a few days the revolution seemed to be winning. Soviet troops pulled out of Budapest and Nagy's government moved far beyond reform communism.
points: Soviet troops withdrew from Budapest between 29 and 31 October. The Soviet government declared on 30 October that it was ready to discuss withdrawing its forces from Hungary, though only the withdrawal from Budapest actually happened.

On 30 October Nagy announced the end of one-party rule and formed a coalition that included non-communist parties: the Smallholders (Zoltán Tildy, Béla Kovács), the Social Democrats and the National Peasant (Petőfi) Party. Kádár was a member.

On 30 October insurgents stormed the party headquarters at Republic Square in Budapest and lynched a number of AVH men and party members. Soviet propaganda later used this violence to paint the revolution as a fascist terror.
Cardinal Mindszenty was freed on 30 October and returned to Budapest, and political prisoners were released. This showed the revolution had freed the regime's best-known victims.
Khrushchev and the Soviet Presidium (the leading committee of the Soviet party) at first leaned towards negotiation, but on 31 October they reversed course and decided to crush the rising.
notes.tip: Do not write that the Communist Party was reduced to a minority in the 30 October coalition. Say one-party rule ended and non-communist parties joined, with Nagy and Kádár still in the cabinet.

notes.h: Neutrality and the Soviet decision: 1-3 November
notes.b: Nagy's declaration on 1 November crossed the line Moscow would accept, and while Hungarians believed negotiations were under way, Moscow prepared the attack.
points: On 1 November Nagy protested to Andropov that new Soviet troops were crossing the border. He then declared Hungary neutral (refusing to side with either bloc) and withdrawing from the Warsaw Pact, and asked UN Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld for UN support.
Neutrality crossed Moscow's line because losing Hungary from the Warsaw Pact threatened the whole Soviet bloc.
The ruling party was refounded as the Hungarian Socialist Workers' Party under Kádár. He left Budapest secretly on the evening of 1 November and was taken to Moscow.
Khrushchev and Malenkov met Tito, the Yugoslav leader, on the island of Brioni on 2-3 November, and Tito agreed that intervention was necessary.
Withdrawal talks continued at Tököl. Maléter, now defence minister, was arrested there by Soviet security forces on the night of 3-4 November, so the negotiations were a trap as well as a delay.
notes.tip: Be exact on 1 November: Nagy's neutrality declaration and Warsaw Pact withdrawal, with his formal appeal to the UN rather than the West. Do not say Suez caused the Soviet decision; it was one factor that made it easier.

notes.b: Early on 4 November a large Soviet force attacked Hungary and removed Nagy's government. This is the date Ordinary Level source questions usually test.
points: The second intervention, codenamed Operation Whirlwind, began early on 4 November 1956 with an overwhelming Soviet force that attacked Budapest and other centres. Sources vary widely on its size, so no exact numbers should be given.

Early that morning Nagy broadcast that Soviet troops were attacking Budapest, that Hungarian troops were fighting and that the government was in its place. He took refuge in the Yugoslav embassy the same day.
Cardinal Mindszenty took refuge in the US embassy on 4 November and stayed there until 1971. This meant the cardinal, freed on 30 October, was again out of Hungarian hands.

Kádár's Revolutionary Worker-Peasant Government was announced on 4 November with Soviet backing, and Kádár entered Budapest with Soviet troops a few days later. This gave the Soviets a Hungarian government to install.
notes.tip: Source questions test the date (4 November), the place (Budapest) and what Nagy's broadcast reported, and why the Soviets acted: to keep Hungary in the bloc. Give one specific fact per short answer.

notes.h: Defeat and the capture of Nagy: November-December
notes.b: Organised fighting ended within days, but workers resisted longer, and Nagy's fate was sealed by a broken promise.
points: Organised armed resistance ended by about 10-11 November. Csepel, an industrial district of Budapest, was among the last areas to fall, which showed how strong support for the uprising was among workers.
The Central Workers' Council of Greater Budapest formed on 14 November. Strikes continued into December, but the workers' councils were suppressed in December 1956.
On 22 November Nagy left the Yugoslav embassy under a written guarantee of safe conduct from Kádár's government. Soviet forces seized him at once and took him to Romania.

Yugoslavia later protested at his seizure from its embassy, even though Tito had accepted the need for intervention. This shows the seizure was resented even by a government that backed the intervention.
notes.tip: Do not say fighting in Budapest went on to the end of November. Organised armed resistance ended by about 10-11 November, while strikes lasted into December. Nagy left the embassy on 22 November under a guarantee from Kádár's government, not a Soviet promise.

notes.h: The West's response: Suez, liberation rhetoric and the UN
notes.b: The West protested but did nothing, and the Suez crisis made that easier. Hungarians who had hoped for help discovered that the Cold War spheres of influence were firmer than the slogans.
points: The Suez crisis overlapped the uprising. Israel invaded Egypt on 29 October 1956, Britain and France issued an ultimatum on 30 October, bombed Egypt from 31 October and landed at Port Said on 5-6 November. A ceasefire followed on 6 November under US pressure.

Suez divided the West, because the USA opposed its own allies over it, and it distracted the UN and world attention from Hungary at a crucial moment. It was one factor that made Soviet action easier, not the cause of it.

US policy had spoken of liberation or rollback of communism, but Secretary of State John Foster Dulles said in a speech on 27 October 1956 that the USA did not regard the satellites as potential military allies.

President Dwight Eisenhower ruled out military intervention. He feared a wider war because of Soviet nuclear power, Hungary lay inside the Soviet sphere, and the US presidential election was on 6 November 1956, when Eisenhower was re-elected.

On 4 November a Security Council resolution was vetoed by the Soviet Union, and an emergency session of the General Assembly then called for Soviet withdrawal. UN observers were refused entry to Hungary, so no observers and no force were ever sent.
A UN special committee reported in 1957 condemning the intervention, but by then it could change nothing. This shows why the UN counted for little: it could report but not act.
notes.tip: Link Suez to Hungary carefully: it overlapped, divided the West and distracted the UN, but it did not cause the Soviet decision. Also keep to the facts that the UN sent nothing and that no Western government promised help.

notes.h: The West's response: Radio Free Europe and the refugees
notes.b: Two other parts of the Western response shaped how people judged it afterwards: the radio broadcasts that raised hopes, and the welcome given to refugees.
points: Radio Free Europe, a US-funded station broadcasting from Munich, encouraged Hungarians. Some of its Hungarian broadcasts encouraged armed resistance and implied that Western help would come.
It was criticised afterwards for raising false hopes. No government had promised help, so the problem was the impression its broadcasts gave, not a formal pledge.
Refugees who reached Austria were welcomed in the West. Ireland received about 500 Hungarian refugees, who were housed at Knockalisheen camp, Co. Clare.
Their arrival was a propaganda victory for the West, and Time magazine named the Hungarian Freedom Fighter its Man of the Year for 1956. It did not change the outcome in Hungary.
Western communist parties lost members and intellectuals after Hungary, which damaged the Soviet Union's reputation among the left. This is an example of how Hungary changed minds outside the bloc.
notes.tip: Questions on Radio Free Europe ask about the charge that it raised false hopes. Say it was US-funded and that its broadcasts implied help, not that the USA openly promised help.

notes.b: The uprising ended in a Soviet victory followed by years of punishment. The human cost is among the most widely quoted measures of its failure.
points: Estimates put the Hungarian dead at about 2,500 to 3,000 and the Soviet dead at about 700. These figures vary between sources, so use them as approximate.

About 200,000 Hungarians fled, most to Austria and some to Yugoslavia. Many were young, skilled or educated, so Hungary lost people it needed. This shows why the exodus mattered: it drained the country of its young.
Afterwards about 20,000 or more people were imprisoned. Executions in connection with 1956 numbered a few hundred, often given as about 230, and continued until about 1961.
Nagy, Maléter and Gimes were hanged on 16 June 1958 after a secret trial whose outcome was decided in advance.

János Kádár, a communist who was interior minister in 1948-50 and who had himself been imprisoned and tortured under Rákosi in 1951-54, led the party from 1956 to 1988. His rule began with repression, which lasted to the early 1960s, and an amnesty for most political prisoners came in 1963.
Kádár then moved to compromise, summed up in his saying of 1961 that whoever is not against us is with us. The New Economic Mechanism, introduced on 1 January 1968, added limited market elements.
Goulash communism is the informal name for Kádár's relatively relaxed, consumer-oriented system from the 1960s. It gave Hungarians more consumer goods as the price of political obedience.
notes.tip: Give casualty figures as ranges with about, never as exact numbers, and do not give a figure for the wounded. For outcomes, link repression under Kádár to the later compromise.

notes.b: The uprising failed mainly because Moscow was determined to keep Hungary, and the Hungarians and the West could not stop it. Strong answers weigh these factors and say which mattered most.
points: Soviet determination was decisive. Hungary's exit from the Warsaw Pact and the end of one-party rule threatened the whole bloc, and Moscow feared that other satellites would follow like falling dominoes.

The Soviets used overwhelming force against insurgents who lacked heavy weapons, outside help and a single command, so the outcome was not in doubt once Moscow chose to attack. This is why the result was never really in doubt.
The West would not act, because of Suez, the risk of nuclear war and the acceptance of spheres of influence (areas each superpower treated as its own). The UN was powerless.
The Hungarians were divided and weak. Nagy followed events rather than leading them, there was no united organisation, and Kádár's defection gave the Soviets a Hungarian government to install.
Poland shows why Hungary was crushed and Poland was not. Gomułka kept communist rule and the Warsaw Pact, so Moscow tolerated him, while Hungary left the pact and ended one-party rule.
notes.tip: The best answers say which cause was decisive: Soviet determination once Hungary left the Warsaw Pact and ended one-party rule. Support it with the West's inaction, Suez, the UN's impotence, the insurgents' lack of weapons and leadership, and Kádár's defection, plus the contrast with Poland.

notes.b: Hungary changed how the Soviet bloc, the Cold War and Hungarians themselves understood the limits of change.
points: For the Soviet bloc, it confirmed the limits of de-Stalinisation and showed that Soviet control would be defended by force. In 1968 Czechoslovak reformers promised to stay in the Warsaw Pact to avoid Hungary's fate. This is why Hungary became the proof that Soviet control rested on force.
For the Cold War, Western talk of liberation was exposed as empty and spheres of influence were tacitly accepted. Soviet prestige was damaged in the West and among the left.
Tension was raised in the same weeks as Suez, because the West was angry at Soviet force. It also eased in a sense, because the West accepted the Soviet sphere in practice.
For Hungary, the memory of 1956 lasted. In January 1989 the reform communist Imre Pozsgay called 1956 a popular uprising rather than a counter-revolution, and Nagy was reburied on 16 June 1989.
On 23 October 1989 the Republic of Hungary was proclaimed, and 23 October is now a national holiday, which marks the collapse of communist authority.
notes.tip: On international tension, pair effects: Soviet force and Western anger and refugee propaganda against the West's tacit acceptance of the Soviet sphere. Paired effects score better than narrative.

notes.h: Assessment: revolution or counter-revolution, success or failure?
notes.b: Historians weigh what the uprising achieved against how quickly it was crushed, and the label chosen shapes judgement of Nagy and of the West.
points: Achievements: within days the uprising forced the withdrawal of Soviet troops from Budapest, a multi-party government and a declaration of neutrality, which no other satellite had achieved. It also gave a few days of freedom.
Limits: it was crushed within days, thousands died, about 200,000 fled and Nagy was executed. It relied on Soviet restraint and had no means of defending itself once Moscow chose force.

Contemporary views: the Kádár regime and the Soviet line called it a counter-revolution by fascists and imperialist agents. The West and later Hungarian opinion saw a national, democratic revolution. These labels matter because each side used its label to justify its own actions.

The insurgents were mostly young workers and students, and most demands were for national independence, free elections and democratic socialism. The evidence does not support the claim of a fascist rising or a bid to restore capitalism.
Later views changed: Pozsgay's 1989 reassessment and Nagy's reburial confirmed the revolution view. Historians still debate Nagy's judgement, his tactics and his naivety about Soviet intentions.
notes.tip: A Higher Level assessment should set achievements against limits as paired points and contrast the contemporary label (counter-revolution against freedom fight) with the later 1989 reassessment.

keyTerms.definition: A state formally independent but dominated politically and militarily by the Soviet Union, as Hungary was after 1945.
The process by which communist parties backed by the Soviet Union took control of eastern European states and remodelled their institutions on the Soviet pattern.
Imre Nagy's programme of 1953 to 1955, which shifted Hungarian policy towards consumer goods, farm relief and looser political controls.
Hungary's announcement on 1 November 1956 that it was leaving the Warsaw Pact and declaring neutrality.
A discussion group of reform-minded Hungarian intellectuals and party members formed in 1955, which helped prepare the uprising.
Elected bodies set up in Hungarian factories and towns during the uprising that demanded workers' control and organised strikes.
The informal name for the more relaxed, consumer-oriented policies of Kádár's Hungary after the uprising.
The Hungarian State Security Authority, the secret police of Rákosi's regime and the main target of popular anger in 1956.
The change of leadership in Poland in October 1956, when Gomułka returned to power and Soviet intervention was avoided; it encouraged Hungarian reformers.
A US-funded radio station broadcasting to eastern Europe, accused of raising false hopes of Western help in Hungary in 1956.

factCards.definition: Nagy was executed on 16 June 1958 after a secret trial, and he was reburied with a state ceremony on 16 June 1989.
A crowd in Budapest pulled down the statue of Stalin on the first day of the uprising, a symbol of the demand for change.

factCards.term: Sixteen points of the students, 22 October 1956
factCards.definition: The Budapest students' list of demands included free elections and the withdrawal of Soviet troops.
On this day Nagy announced neutrality and withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact, and appealed to the United Nations.
Soviet forces returned in strength on 4 November 1956 and crushed the uprising in Budapest and other towns.
Kádár left Budapest on 1 November, and a rival government under him was proclaimed on 4 November, based at Szolnok and backed by Soviet troops.

factCards.term: Nagy's refuge in the Yugoslav embassy
factCards.definition: Nagy sheltered in the Yugoslav embassy in Budapest from 4 November until he left on 22 November 1956 under a Soviet promise of safe passage.
About 200,000 Hungarians fled to Austria and beyond; the exact figure varies between sources.
Israel invaded Egypt on 29 October 1956 and Britain and France attacked Egypt from 31 October, drawing Western attention away from Hungary.

factCards.term: Radio Free Europe during the uprising
factCards.definition: The Western-funded station broadcast encouragement to Hungarians, but no Western government sent military help.

factCards.term: Why did Nagy's neutrality declaration provoke the USSR?
factCards.definition: Leaving the Warsaw Pact threatened the Soviet security system and might have encouraged other satellites to follow, so Moscow intervened.

factCards.term: Hungary 1956: who led the second government
factCards.definition: János Kádár, who left Nagy's government on 1 November, formed a rival government with Soviet backing, and became prime minister on 4 November.
